plain_english: When I say that I do nothing for the sake of pleasure, I'm talking about the wise man — the only person you admit can truly enjoy pleasure. But I don't call anyone wise if they can be conquered by anything, especially by pleasure. If pleasure has power over him, how will he resist hard work, danger, poverty, and all the troubles that surround human life? How will he face death or pain? How will he handle the chaos of the world and fight against so many fierce enemies, if he's been defeated by such a weak opponent? He'll do whatever pleasure tells him to do. Can't you see how many terrible things it will make him do?
original_excerpt: When I say that I do nothing for the sake of pleasure, I allude to that wise man, whom alone you admit to be capable of pleasure: now I do not call a man wise who is overcome by anything, let alone by pleasure: yet, if engrossed by pleasure, how will he resist toil, danger, want, and all the ills which surround and threaten the life of man? How will he bear the sight of death or of pain? How will he endure the tumult of the world, and make head against so many most active foes, if he be conquered by so effeminate an antagonist? He will do whatever pleasure advises him: well, do you not see how many things it will advise him to do?

plain_english: "It won't," says our opponent, "be able to give him bad advice, because it's combined with virtue." But don't you see what a weak kind of highest good this must be if it needs a guardian to make sure it stays good? And how can virtue rule pleasure if virtue follows pleasure around? The follower takes orders — the commander gives them. Are you really putting the one who should command in second place? According to your school of thought, virtue gets the dignified job of taste-testing pleasures first. But we'll see if virtue is still virtue when people treat her with such disrespect. If she abandons her proper position, she can no longer keep her proper name.
original_excerpt: "It will not," says our adversary, "be able to give him any bad advice, because it is combined with virtue?" Again, do you not see what a poor kind of highest good that must be which requires a guardian to ensure its being good at all? and how is virtue to rule pleasure if she follows it, seeing that to follow is the duty of a subordinate, to rule that of a commander? do you put that which commands in the background? According to your school, virtue has the dignified office of preliminary taster of pleasures. We shall, however, see whether virtue still remains virtue among those who treat her with such contempt, for if she leaves her proper station she can no longer keep her proper name:

plain_english: But let me stick to the point. I can show you many men who are drowning in pleasures — men Fortune has blessed with everything. You'd have to admit these are bad men. Look at Nomentanus and Apicius. They devour all the "good things" from sea and land. They parade the entire animal kingdom across their dinner tables. Picture them lying on beds of roses, gloating over their feasts. They delight their ears with music, their eyes with shows, their tongues with exotic flavors. Their whole bodies are pampered with soft, soothing touches. And so their noses won't feel left out, they perfume the very rooms where they worship luxury. You'd say these men live surrounded by pleasures. Yet they're miserable — because they're taking pleasure in things that aren't actually good.
original_excerpt: in the meanwhile, to keep to the point, I will show you many men beset by pleasures, men upon whom Fortune has showered all her gifts, whom you must needs admit to be bad men. Look at Nomentanus and Apicius, who digest all the good things, as they call them, of the sea and land, and review upon their tables the whole animal kingdom. Look at them as they lie on beds of roses gloating over their banquet, delighting their ears with music, their eyes with exhibitions, their palates with flavours: their whole bodies are titillated with soft and soothing applications, and lest even their nostrils should be idle, the very place in which, they solemnize the rites of luxury is scented with various perfumes. You will say that these men live in the midst of pleasures. Yet they are ill at ease, because they take pleasure in what is not good.
